topics.title: Rectangular Cartesian Coordinates in 2 Dimensions
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: draw and label the Cartesian plane. (k, s)
read and plot points on the Cartesian plane/coordinate grid. (k, s)

choose and uses appropriate scale for a bi-variate data set. (u, s, v/a)

body.text: When a visitor asks for your seat in class, you might say "row 3, desk 5". Two numbers are enough to find one place. Maps of Kampala, seating plans for a school assembly and computer screens all use this idea. In mathematics we use a grid called the Cartesian plane.
The Cartesian plane is made from two number lines that cross at right angles. The horizontal line is the x-axis. The vertical line is the y-axis. They cross at the origin, the point (0, 0).

On the x-axis, numbers to the right of the origin are positive and numbers to the left are negative. On the y-axis, numbers above the origin are positive and numbers below are negative. The axes divide the plane into four parts called quadrants.

items: Draw a horizontal line across the page and a vertical line up the page, crossing near the middle.
Mark equal steps along each line, for example one step for every 1 cm.
Number the steps: 1, 2, 3 to the right and up; −1, −2, −3 to the left and down.
Write x at the right end of the horizontal axis and y at the top of the vertical axis.

body.text: Every point has two coordinates, written in brackets as (x, y). The x-coordinate comes first and tells you how far to move across. The y-coordinate comes second and tells you how far to move up or down. A helpful saying is "along the corridor, then up the stairs".

body.speech: the point P has coordinates x comma y

body.title: Plot the points A(3, 2), B(−2, 4), C(−3, −1) and D(2, −3)
steps: A(3, 2): start at the origin, move 3 to the right, then 2 up. A is in the first quadrant.
B(−2, 4): move 2 to the left, then 4 up. B is in the second quadrant.
C(−3, −1): move 3 to the left, then 1 down. C is in the third quadrant.
D(2, −3): move 2 to the right, then 3 down. D is in the fourth quadrant.
Mark each point with a small cross and write its letter beside it.

body.text: To read a point, do the same in reverse. Drop a line from the point straight down or up to the x-axis and read the number. Then go across to the y-axis and read the number there. A point on the x-axis always has y = 0, and a point on the y-axis always has x = 0.

If you know some corners of a shape, its properties help you find the rest. In a rectangle, opposite sides are equal and parallel, and all corners are right angles. In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and parallel.

body.title: Find the fourth corner of a rectangle
steps: Three corners of rectangle PQRS are P(−3, 1), Q(2, 1) and R(2, 4).
P and Q have the same y-coordinate, so PQ is a horizontal side.
Q and R have the same x-coordinate, so QR is a vertical side 3 units long.
S must be 3 units above P, so S has the same x-coordinate as P and the same y-coordinate as R.

body.title: Find the fourth corner of a parallelogram
steps: Three corners of parallelogram ABCD are A(0, 0), B(4, 0) and C(5, 3).
To go from B to C, you move 1 to the right and 3 up.
AD must be parallel and equal to BC, so make the same move from A.
Start at A(0, 0), move 1 right and 3 up.

body.text: Bivariate data means two measurements taken for each person or thing, such as the age and height of each learner. Each pair of measurements becomes one point. A graph of these points is called a scatter graph.

A scale tells you how much each step on an axis stands for. Choose a scale that is easy to read, such as 1, 2, 5 or 10 units per centimetre. The graph should fill most of the page. If the values do not start near zero, start the axis at a sensible value and show a small zigzag at the start of the axis.

body.title: Choose scales for ages and heights
steps: Kyomuhendo measures five children. Their ages are from 5 to 15 years and their heights are from 100 cm to 180 cm.
The page is about 18 cm wide and 24 cm tall.
Ages cover 10 years. A scale of 1 cm for 1 year uses 10 cm across the page. That fits well.
Heights cover 80 cm. A scale of 2 cm for every 10 cm of height uses 16 cm up the page.
Start the height axis at 100 cm with a zigzag, and number it 100, 110, 120 and so on up to 180.
Plot each child as a point (age, height).

body.title: Four in a line
body.text: Play in pairs on a coordinate grid drawn from −5 to 5 on both axes. Take turns to call out a point, such as (2, −3), and plot it in your own colour. Write down each point you call. The first player to get four points in a straight line wins the round. Afterwards, look at the coordinates of your four points. What do you notice?
Two corners of a square are at (2, 1) and (6, 3). Where could the other two corners be? Discuss in your group. How many different squares can you find?
The x-axis is horizontal and the y-axis is vertical. They meet at the origin (0, 0). A point is written (x, y): across first, then up or down. Choose a scale that is easy to read and fills the page.
